reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
clinicalPearls: A rare disorder of progressive, spontaneous massive osteolysis with replacement of bone by proliferating thin-walled vascular and lymphatic channels
Bone is resorbed and effectively disappears on serial radiographs, giving rise to the vanishing or phantom bone description
Can affect any bone but has a predilection for the shoulder girdle, skull, spine, pelvis, and ribs, and it may cross joints and normal anatomical boundaries
Presents with insidious pain, weakness, deformity, or a pathological fracture, sometimes discovered incidentally
Involvement of the ribs, spine, or thoracic duct can lead to chylothorax, a serious and potentially fatal complication
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring biopsy showing angiomatous or lymphangiomatous proliferation and exclusion of infection, malignancy, and other osteolytic disease
Management is individualised and may combine antiresorptive therapy, agents targeting abnormal vascular and lymphatic proliferation, radiotherapy, and surgical stabilisation
reference.pathophysiology: Gorham-Stout disease is characterised by uncontrolled proliferation of vascular and lymphatic endothelial channels within bone that progressively replace and destroy the osseous matrix. The abnormal vessels and associated osteoclastic activity dissolve bone in a relentless, often locally aggressive fashion, though the process does not metastasise. The trigger is not fully understood, but dysregulated lymphangiogenesis and angiogenesis, with increased osteoclast sensitivity to humoral factors, are thought central. When the disease reaches the thoracic cavity or thoracic duct, abnormal lymphatic channels can leak, producing chylous effusions that carry significant morbidity and mortality.
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic bone disease or multiple myeloma
Primary bone malignancy such as haemangioendothelioma
additionalInvestigations: Serial plain radiographs documenting progressive osteolysis and disappearance of bone
MRI and CT to define soft-tissue and vascular-lymphatic involvement
Bone biopsy demonstrating angiomatous or lymphangiomatous tissue and excluding malignancy
Chest imaging and pleural fluid analysis where chylothorax is suspected
Inflammatory markers, serum calcium, and bone turnover markers
Screening for associated lymphatic anomalies in adjacent tissues
redFlags: Dyspnoea and a chylous pleural effusion indicating thoracic duct or rib involvement
Rapidly progressive osteolysis threatening the spine with instability or cord compromise
Pathological fracture in a weight-bearing or load-critical bone
Skull-base involvement with neurological deficit or cerebrospinal fluid leak
reference.prognosis: The course is unpredictable; disease may stabilise spontaneously or progress relentlessly, and prognosis is generally good when confined to an extremity but markedly worse with thoracic involvement and chylothorax.
pitfalls: Labelling the osteolysis as malignancy or infection without appropriate biopsy
Underestimating the risk of chylothorax when ribs, spine, or thorax are affected
Assuming stabilisation is permanent and stopping surveillance too early
Attempting isolated surgery without addressing the underlying vascular-lymphatic process, risking recurrence
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
Peer-reviewed reviews of Gorham-Stout disease and complex lymphatic anomalies
management: Give antiresorptive therapy with bisphosphonates to inhibit the osteoclastic bone destruction
Use anti-angiogenic and antiproliferative agents such as interferon-alpha and the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus to target the abnormal vascular and lymphatic proliferation
Deliver localised radiotherapy to halt progression at aggressive or surgically inaccessible sites
Provide surgical stabilisation, resection and reconstruction with bone grafting or orthopaedic fixation for pathological fracture, deformity or instability
Manage chylothorax aggressively with drainage, a low-fat medium-chain-triglyceride diet, thoracic duct intervention and sirolimus, given its high mortality
Monitor osteolysis with serial imaging and coordinate multidisciplinary metabolic bone, orthopaedic, interventional radiology, thoracic surgery and lymphatic-anomaly care
